Checked 2d993f7 and the companion fix looks right — `structured` is captured by the onSuccess closure outside the loop (prompt.ts:1266), so without the `structured = undefined` on the continue path the check at :1307 would attach the previous turn's output to the next assistant message. Also confirmed `lastUser` is re-derived from fresh msgs each iteration (:1096), so StructuredOutput only gets re-injected when the new prompt itself carries the format.

One FYI, not an issue: with this, a steer landing between onSuccess capture and the structured break means the run resolves with the steer's reply — the structured value stays persisted on the earlier assistant message but isn't what the run returns to the original caller. Seems like the right trade vs. handing the queued prompt the dead turn's message, just flagging it.

Thanks for the report. We can't reproduce this as described because the version, invocation, and error do not line up with the shipped runtimes:

- In OpenCode 1.18.30's experimental Code Mode, discovery is exposed as `tools.$codemode.search(...)`. Calling bare `search(...)` there would fail as an unknown identifier, not as `Unknown tool 'search'`.
- In OpenCode V2, discovery is the bare built-in `search(...)`. The exact error quoted here is what V2 returns when `tools.search(...)` is called instead.

So the reported bare `search(...)` snippet and the quoted error cannot originate from the same official runtime described in the environment. The environment also lists both the 1.18.30 release and a `0.0.0-beta-19242` runtime snapshot, which suggests the CLI, background service, harness, or captured invocation may be coming from different installations.

Closing as can't reproduce. If this still occurs, please provide the raw `execute` input and complete output, together with the version reported by the process/background service actually handling that session. That would let us identify which runtime is executing the call.

Same wall, different Qwen — got bitten by this with qwen3.8-flash on the /v1/messages route this week and managed to pin down the threshold pretty exactly, so here's the extra data point before I close the book on it.

Background: I have a long-running session that had spent most of its life on mimo-v2.5, so its message history still carried a handful of image blocks from earlier turns (~1400x2000, a few MB of base64 in total). I switched it to qwen3.8-flash to continue the work, and the very first request in that model failed with:

Bad Request: {"model":"qwen3.8-flash"}

That's literally the whole response body — 25 bytes, application/json, straight from the gateway. No error text, nothing that says "too large", nothing that says "images". Retrying 100% reproduces it. Switching the same session to mimo-v2.5 kept going with the exact same history, so the payload is fine on a different route through the same gateway.

I bisected it with throwaway opencode run calls in fresh sessions using the same scan files:
- 1 to 4 images (body ≈5.75 MB total) → fine
- 5 images (body ≈6.85 MB) → 400, 3/3
- 8 tiny 64x64 PNGs (body ~35 KB) → fine

So it's the cumulative body size, not the image count, and the cutoff lines up with @AkariSam's 6291456 exactly. The difference is the error handling: on qwen3.7-plus the upstream at least passed back "Exceeded limit on max bytes to request body". On the Anthropic-style route for qwen3.8-flash that message gets swallowed and you just get the model name echoed back. Cost me two days of thinking my config was broken.

The second failure mode is nastier, because it doesn't look like a size error at all. When the oversized images arrive in message history rather than as a fresh attachment, the request sometimes starts streaming normally and then dies mid-turn with:

AI_TypeValidationError: Type validation failed: Value: {}.
[{ code: invalid_union, note: "No matching discriminator",
   discriminator: type, path: [ "type" ] }]

You get a couple of reasoning chunks first, then the stream emits something schema-invalid, the assistant message is left as an error, and every later turn replays the same history and dies again — the session is bricked until you /undo the image turns or change model. (This is basically the third gap @NoahBPeterson described above: images sit in history and nothing evicts or downsizes them, so the next request is doomed before it's sent.)

Versions: opencode 1.18.27, Windows 11, model opencode-go/qwen3.8-flash, endpoint https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages.

Minimal repro: opencode run -m opencode-go/qwen3.8-flash --file a.png --file b.png --file c.png --file d.png --file e.png "describe these" with five ~1 MB page screenshots. Same command with four files succeeds.

Would really like (a) the gateway to pass the provider's "request body too large" through instead of echoing the model param, and (b) images in history to count toward overflow handling / get evicted, so a normal screenshot loop doesn't silently brick a session.

had a look and i don't think this is a bug, the snippet just doesn't return anything. `execute` uses the program's return value as the result, and when there's no `return` it takes the last top-level expression, which here is `console.log(result)`. that's `undefined`, and `toData` in `packages/codemode/src/data.ts` turns an undefined execution result into `null`. so you get `null` and then whatever was logged.

Read through the sanitize→resend chain and it holds up on our side — `to-llm-message.ts:168` lifts `item.state` into `providerMetadata`, and `lowerReasoning` (open-responses.ts:529) drops the part entirely once state is undefined, so the stale item really does leave the request.

One durability concern: `RecoverStaleReasoning` updates `SessionMessageTable` rows directly without publishing anything on the Bus. That table is a projection — `replaySessionProjection` (session-runner.test.ts:715) deletes the rows and re-folds everything from EventTable, so any later rebuild would resurrect the old state with `reasoningEncryptedContent`/`itemId` and the stale-reasoning error can come back after a replay. Would it make sense to go through the event path instead, the way normal assistant updates reach the projector (projector.ts:232)?

Related: the post-replay assertion only matches `{type, text}`, so it can't tell the state came back — worth asserting state is gone there.

Minor: the update loop rewrites every assistant message in the window, even untouched ones. Filtering to the messages `sanitizeReasoning` actually changed would keep it cheap.

this isn't really opencode holding onto old values, a process gets its env when it starts and windows doesn't push PATH changes into processes that are already running. same reason the Git Bash window you had open won't see the new PATH either.

on 2.0.3 the cli snapshots its env at launch (`Env.session()` in `packages/cli/src/env.ts`) and the tui sends it to the session through `session.environment` when you open it, and the shell tool spawns with that. so you shouldn't lose anything by restarting, open a fresh terminal and run `opencode --continue` (or pick the session again) and the new PATH goes into that session. history is stored, it's not dropped on restart.

an actual in-app refresh would mean reading the user/system env out of the registry on windows and deciding how it merges with what the session already has, which seems like a design call for the team more than a quick PR.

This is the same root cause as #48224, but in TUI mode rather than web sessions.

**Key difference from #48224:**
- #48224 reports `browser.disconnected` errors in web sessions
- Here the issue is TUI (terminal) mode: the LLM sees 44 `browser.*` tools in the catalog and attempts to call them (e.g., `browser.screenshot`, `browser.navigate`), wasting tokens and producing no useful result — since TUI has no browser engine at all

**Same project, different modes:**
- Desktop app: browser tools work correctly ✅
- TUI mode: browser tools are non-functional but still advertised ❌

The fundamental fix is the same: gate the browser tool catalog on actual runtime browser availability. In TUI (and web sessions where no desktop browser is connected), these tools should be excluded from the catalog presented to the model.

Closing in favor of #48224.
Duplicate of #48224 — same root cause (browser tools exposed without browser engine), different context (TUI mode). Consolidating there.

To add a practical use case to this discussion:

I frequently need to configure proxy settings (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, etc.) or other environment variables that should only apply to OpenCode — not to my entire system. For example:

- Proxy configuration for API requests (providers, MCP servers)
- Custom `PATH` entries for project-specific CLI tools
- API keys or tokens scoped to a single project

**What I think would help:**

1. **Config-level environment overrides** — Allow setting environment variables in `opencode.jsonc` (global or project-level) that are applied to all sessions spawned by OpenCode. Something like:

   ```jsonc
   {
     "environment": {
       "HTTP_PROXY": "http://127.0.0.1:7890",
       "PATH": "${PATH};D:\\Tools\\gh\\bin"
     }
   }
   ```

2. **TUI/Desktop env editor** — A built-in UI (accessible via a shortcut or command) to view and edit environment variables for the current session or project, without needing to restart OpenCode.

3. **Per-session env refresh** — When starting a new session (not restarting OpenCode), re-read the current system environment and merge it with any config-level overrides. This way, even if the running OpenCode process has stale env vars, a fresh session picks up the latest.

This would solve the proxy use case cleanly: I set `HTTP_PROXY` in my project's `opencode.jsonc`, and every session in that project uses it for all outbound requests — regardless of what the host terminal's environment looks like.

Quick follow-up question: if I modify the system environment variables and then run `opencode service restart`, would the new sessions pick up the updated environment without losing existing session history? Or does the service also snapshot the env at its own launch time?

yeah the service snapshots its env too. it gets spawned as a detached child of whichever opencode process starts it, with that process's env plus anything you set through `opencode service set env` (`spawnServiceContender` in `packages/client/src/service-contender.ts`). so `opencode service restart` run from a terminal you opened after changing the vars gives the service the new env, and history is fine since sessions are stored, not held by the service process. the cli restart does close persistent terminals though. the tui's `/restart` won't help here, that respawns the service from the tui process which still has the old env.

the catch is the shell tool. once the tui has pushed a session env it spawns with `sessionEnvironment ?? process.env` (`packages/core/src/shell.ts`), and an open tui re-pushes its own launch snapshot as soon as it reconnects. so a service restart updates what the service does itself, provider requests and mcp servers, but bash commands in a tui that was already open still get the old PATH. for those you need to reopen the tui from a new terminal, `opencode --continue`.

for the proxy case `opencode service set env HTTP_PROXY http://127.0.0.1:7890` already exists and sticks across restarts, same caveat that it applies to the service process and not to shell commands in a tui session.

I saw PR #47680 (`tool.snapshot` plugin hook) which provides the capability to hide tools per request. That's a useful mechanism, but I don't think a plugin is the right solution for this specific problem.

**The core issue is:** OpenCode already knows whether it's running in TUI, web, or desktop mode. It should automatically filter out browser tools when no browser engine is available — this should be built-in behavior, not something users need to install a plugin for.

Requiring a plugin to prevent the LLM from attempting non-functional tool calls feels backwards. The `tool.snapshot` hook is great for **user-defined** tool filtering (e.g., custom workflows, role-based tool access), but platform-level capability detection should be handled by the core itself.

**What I'd expect:**
- TUI mode → browser tools automatically excluded from the catalog
- Web session without desktop connection → same
- Desktop with browser attached → browser tools available

No plugin needed, no user configuration needed. OpenCode should just do the right thing based on its runtime environment.

The plugin hook is still valuable for advanced use cases, but please don't let it be the excuse for not fixing the built-in behavior.

I think the tool call is actually working here, and the `null` is coming from the script rather than from MCP.

In `packages/opencode/src/tool/code-mode.ts`, the tool output is built from the script's **return value**, and `console.log` output is appended separately under `Logs:`:

```ts
const withLogs = (text: string) =>
  text.length > 0 ? `${text}\n\nLogs:\n${logs.join("\n")}` : `Logs:\n${logs.join("\n")}`
```

Your script is:

```js
const result = await tools["api-testing"].env_list();
console.log(result);
```

That returns nothing, so the script's value is `undefined`, normalized to `null` on the way out of the sandbox (`copyOut(..., undefinedAsNull)` in `packages/codemode/src/tool-runtime.ts`) and serialized as `null`. Meanwhile the array under `Logs:` is exactly what `console.log(result)` printed — which means `result` did hold the parsed response, not `null`.

Ending the script with the value should give you what you expect:

```js
const result = await tools["api-testing"].env_list();
return result;
```

For what it's worth, `projectMcpResult` in the same file does already handle the case you describe — it collects `text` blocks and returns `text.join("\n")`, and prefers `structuredContent` when present.

If you do return the value and still get `null`, then something else is going on and it's worth digging further — in that case the `content` array your server sends for one specific call would help.
